Figure 2:Two-stage visual state pretraining.Stage 1 trains an encoderEEfrom scratch with four objectives on shared patch tokens.
Stage 2 initializes a student fromEEand keepsEEfrozen as the teacher.
Given student tokens from an augmented cropAAand query tokens encoding position and relative scale, a predictor regresses standardized teacher tokens from a clean cropBB.
Only patches ofBBwhose centers lie insideAAcontribute to the loss.
After training, the predictor is discarded and the refined student serves as ALPS.

Figure 3:The LIBERO state probe.(a) A lightweight probe reads frozen tokens from the last 16 frames to estimate the current scene state from observations alone (readout) or predict the state 1 or 3 s ahead given robot actions (prediction).
(b) State predictions 3 s ahead from ALPS and SigLIP 2, overlaid on the frame observed 3 s later, shown on the held-out LIBERO-Spatial episode with the median error difference between the two encoders.
(c) Per-object position errors at this step, the manipulated bowl’s error over the episode, and its mean error across 50 held-out episodes.

Figure 4:Reconstruction from frozen tokens.Following the input column, each column shows the evaluation decoder’s output from one encoder’s frozen tokens, labeled with its meanℓ1\ell_{1}error across the 1,000 held-out ImageNet images.
The rows show the first three images from a random sample (Fig.S7).ALPS, OpenVision 3, MAE, and VC-1 retain sharp edges and textures.
C-RADIOv3 and DINOv3 preserve spatial layout with softer detail, while SigLIP 2, PE-Core, and CLIP mainly recover coarse structure.

Figure 6:Rendered world-model predictions on PushT(window 834, largest true motion among 200 windows).
The top row shows ground-truth frames; lower rows show each encoder’s evaluation-decoder outputs from real current tokens (green) and open-loop predicted tokens given recorded actions (blue).
Mean errors:Tab.S15; full sequence:Fig.S4.

Figure S1:Closed-loop rollouts of policies trained on frozen ALPS tokensacross two tasks each from LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, shown with their language instructions.
We display the first two tasks (in canonical task order) whose recorded rollout succeeded; overall, 15 of the 20 recorded rollouts across the two suites (one per task) succeeded.

Figure S2:Planning on PushT with a world model over frozen tokens: start, goal, and final states for each encoder on the first four goals ofTab.3.
Labels indicate executed simulator steps; dashed outlines mark the target block and agent poses.
This visualization comes from a separate run of the same CEM planner; because action sampling is stochastic, DINOv2 misses goal 1 here despite succeeding in the main evaluation ofTab.3.

Figure S3:Executed PushT rollouts for the four goals inFig.S2, comparing ALPS and DINOv2: six frames from the initial state to the final evaluated state, followed by the goal image (dashed outlines mark the target block and agent poses).
DINOv2 misses goal 1 in this rollout (Fig.S2).

Figure S4:Rendered world-model predictions across encoders on PushT window 834, ranked first by our motion criterion (Sec.S2).

Row annotations report 5-step LPIPS against the true frame alongside block position and angle errors read by the probe ofTab.4.
